segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The man is my dad. And the thing he cannot let go of is a high school basketball game from 1978. I found out about the game when I was a kid. My mom had saved this old newspaper clipping, or maybe it was a yearbook. But either way, there is this picture of my dad on a basketball court. And when I brought it to her, she told me not to ask my dad about it. And so, I never brought it up. But it bugged me, because basketball is the one thing my dad and I share.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Of my four siblings, I'm the only one who fell for the game like my dad. I loved being on the court; the sound of squeaking shoes, creaking floors; the way the entire space of the gym would vibrate; the way my body would twist, and turn, and pivot to the basket. I loved basketball, but I also loved the attention my dad gave me because of it. In the car after games, we'd annoy the hell out of the rest of my family by dissecting my every move, figuring out what I could improve on, what I did well. It was like we were speaking our own language. Together, we laid out big dreams for my future-- club teams, high school star, college, the WNBA.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: But when I got to high school, I cared less about the game. Our postgame talk stopped feeling like conversations and started sounding like lectures. I started to dread the car rides home.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And there's one ride for my junior year of high school that I still think about all the time. I was walking to my dad's car after the game. And as soon as I closed the door, it started. Why didn't you do this? You need to do this. How could you do this? As I listen to the steady rhythm of my dad's critique, I realized, these lectures weren't about me or what I wanted. They were about him.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So I did something I had never done before. Shut the fuck up, I shouted. He was taken aback for a moment, and then stony silence, waiting for an apology. But it was an apology I wouldn't give. I told him that I didn't want to talk about basketball with him anymore. And if that's all he wanted to talk about, we didn't need to talk. So we didn't. For over a year, we barely spoke to each other.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: A lot of time has passed. I haven't picked up a ball in forever. Neither has my dad. The silence is long gone. But there's something that hasn't been repaired. Nowadays, we just exchange basketball pleasantries. Did you watch that game? How does the team look this year? LeBron, LeBron, LeBron.

segments.text: Watching myself 40 years ago playing basketball, revisiting those moments. But my teammates said that I played very like a bear, or beast, or whatever. I would like to see that part of the video. Versus what I perceive that I did not play very well. So from retrospective, I would like to see that version-- the beast.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The beast? The Mississippi Slammer?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Well, you know, I'd take anything right now.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Here we go.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: A grainy black and white court comes into focus. Players zoomed towards the basket and layup lines. Lots of them have afros.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Can you tell which one is me?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Um, not yet. Well, it's all over the place.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And then I see him. It's his body language, so like my little brother's that it gives him away.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Is this you?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: That's me, yeah.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Is that you?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yes, that's me.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: He's sporting a white jersey and teeny, tight white shorts that are very shy of his knees. Tube socks and high top sneakers-- the shoes make me cringe. Ankle support apparently was not a thing. And he's way skinnier than I've ever known him.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You're so teeny.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yeah, all 189 pounds of me.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: When was the last time you were 189 pounds.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yeah, in high school.

segments.speaker: TV Announcer
segments.text: Hold on, this game is underway.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The teams line up at the big [INAUDIBLE] half court for the jump ball. My dad loses the jump. The other team picks the ball up on the court, fires off a quick jumper that bounces off the rim. My dad's team takes the ball down, and throws up a shot, and also misses. My dad grabs the rebound.

segments.speaker: TV Announcer
segments.text: Bobby Berry has it.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Bobby Berry-- that's my dad. The funny thing is that as he watches, he seems to forget that he knows how this game ends. And he's watching it like any other game on TV.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Come on.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: My dad's team scores the first two baskets. It's 4-0. But the lead doesn't seem to matter to him. He's already down on himself.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What are you seeing right now?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Me standing.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Um, I don't go to the ball. I go away from the ball. Watch the ball come to this side. Now watch where I go-- opposite side of the ball.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I start to say things like, it just started. It's not that bad. I'm pointing out every good thing he does.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Look, you just got an offensive rebound.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And I'm so busy talking, I almost miss the play that's haunted my dad.

segments.speaker: TV Announcer
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] Tony Daniel high post drives around his hand, puts it up-- no good.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You got the board.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: There it is.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Is that the shot? Was that it?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yes. Yeah, that was the shot.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You want to--

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE] No, I don't want to see it again. Once is enough.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The play is over so quick. It's just a second on the screen. And the thing is after that shot, his teammate rebounds the ball and puts it in. In other words, the miss-- it didn't matter. They still score.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: But it did matter to my dad. He never really recovers. And for the rest of the game, he misses shot after shot. Though it's not all bad. He makes a monster block on the next play. Though watching, he barely seems to notice. Next play down, he's fouled on the shot. So he gets two free throws.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yeah, free throws! That's what I mean.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You made your free throw.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: I missed a shot, two feet away.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I keep trying to get him to see what his teammates saw. He won't.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: You guys are up by quite a bit.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yeah, I know. That's the point. We lost.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: At halftime, it's 22-21. My dad's team is up by one. But by the second half, it's as if my dad remembers what he's watching and how it ends. No more yelling, he just sort of sits hand over mouth, quiet.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And this is where I start to think, wait, is he mad at me? I start to worry that this was a terrible idea. This isn't going to make him feel better. Rather than think about one mistake in a game from 40 years ago, he can now watch 40 minutes of mistakes.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The game remains close. And I can see what his teammates are saying about him being a beast. He's pulling down lots of rebounds. He is the reason they're still in the game. But he's not scoring much. Then, in the fourth quarter, their opponent pulls ahead by just a few. And my dad's team can't catch up. It's over.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The camera shows one final moment of my dad. It zooms in on him before he heads into the locker room. He leans down, wrapping his arms around his coach, consoling him. My father at the kitchen table has far less compassion for himself.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: How are you feeling?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Uh, depressed. But I can't do anything about it. It's like I said. It's sad to see that game over again, that's for sure. And I didn't-- still, I feel the same way. I felt that I did not play very well, the way I felt that I should.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: My dad finally got to see how this moment actually looked from the outside. And it didn't change anything for him.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: You can't imagine that things were different. The tape proves the way I felt that I played is what the tape shows.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: When we were watching, I worried that I'd upset my dad. I had.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Well, you're reopening a wound.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Me?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Yes. Why are you making me watch this game?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Does it make you that upset?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: I'm not upset. It just reopens it, and making me revisit it is not necessarily making me--

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: See, I think my hope was that by watching it, it would make you feel better. Like, you could let go of it.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: The only way I probably can ever let go of it is go back into time and reverse everything. And that's not going to happen.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Is that really what it would take?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: I think that's probably what it would take.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I think it makes me upset that you feel upset or that you feel depressed about this. Because it just--

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: I know it's just a game.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: It's not that it's just a game. It's just that it's so long ago and that like, yes, it's sad--

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Oh, believe me. In my life, I'm a very blessed and happy man.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Well, that's it, though. That's exactly it. It just feels like this is such an insignificant thing to all of the great shit that you have going on in your life.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Watch the language.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Sorry.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: My dad did point out one positive thing in the video that I couldn't have noticed.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: You know what I said to my coach?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What did you say?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: I'm sorry, sir.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What were you sorry for?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Losing the game. Now I gotta go. I never told anybody what I said to my coach.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What did he say back?

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: No, you played your ass off.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: At this point, we've been talking for close to an hour. And I realized what I'm doing isn't working. I've been keeping things positive, trying to make my dad see something else-- sugar coating it. And you know what I hate? I hate when people sugar coat things.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The truth was, he was right. He didn't play well. That dunk-- he really did pass the ball over the rim, instead of just dropping it in. After that, he only scored three points. He played exactly the way he told me not to play for most of my basketball career, hanging out around the basket, hands down. He missed easy put backs. He did rebound well, but without him as a threat offensively, his team suffered.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I think he's absolutely right. If he'd played better, they would have won. Maybe what he needed wasn't to see himself differently. What he needed was for someone to see him just the way he is.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I mean, to be frank, it was not a great game for you.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: It wasn't a great-- it was a horrible game for me.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: But I wanted you to also see yourself play basketball. And I think I was hoping that it would be different than you imagined.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Why would you think that?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Because I always imagined that I played like shit. [LAUGHS] And I like to think I don't look that bad on tape.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: Well, you see?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: We chatted a little longer, my dad looking drained-- I think a little sad. It was late, and the Raptors were about to play the Bucks. So I left my dad to watch his game. I spent the evening pretending to read, but really, I was worried about what I just did. The next morning, my dad told me he had something he wanted to say.

segments.speaker: Bobby Berry
segments.text: You know, I actually felt a sense of relief after watching the game with you. I don't think I would've watched it, to tell you the truth. So getting through that with someone that you care and for them to sit there, and watch, and just be brutally honest, like you said, that I played like shit-- excuse my language. But those things are important.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: And that's what I wanted, to talk to my dad about the important things. And since I started this conversation, we've been doing that more and more. We've talked about his childhood in Mississippi, about his health, like how dialysis is so depleting, and about his own parents and how he sees them.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Our conversations are not always this deep. But you know what they're not always about? They're not always about basketball.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Emanuele Berry is one of the producers of our show. A version of this story appeared on The Nod, a podcast that tells stories about black culture that you won't hear anywhere else. Like, LeVar Burton discussing the love life of black Star Trek characters. You can find The Nod wherever you get your podcasts.

segments.speaker: Zack McDermott
segments.text: Coconut oil on that ass now.
